title: Pandu and the deer
hookLine: King Pandu, out hunting, shoots a deer that turns out to be a sage, and one quick arrow bears fruit for the rest of his life
carry: karma: even a quick arrow bears fruit
tomorrow: Kunti tells Pandu a secret: words a sage gave her as a girl.

cards: A stag and a doe, together in a quiet forest clearing. A king on the hunt sees them through the trees, draws his bow, and shoots, quickly, without warning. The arrows strike the stag, and it falls.
Then, lying in the grass, it speaks in a man's voice. King Pandu has just shot a sage.

teach.b: Back up a little. At her self-choice, the princess Kunti chose Pandu for her husband, and Bhishma brought him a second wife, Madri. Pandu won wars, filled the treasury, then went to the forest with both wives to hunt.

That's where he meets the deer. The stag is a sage named Kindama, who had taken a deer's form to be with his wife. As he dies, he says: even a king who may hunt should not strike a creature at a moment like this.
You've killed me in a moment of love. So when you go to your wife in love, you will die. And Pandu has no son yet.
This is karma, one of Hinduism's biggest ideas, in a single arrow.
Karma means action, and every action bears fruit, sooner or later, in this life or another. Not a punishment from an angry god; more like a seed that has to grow. Pandu's arrow took an instant.
Its fruit took the rest of his life. But watch what he does next, because that's karma too. He doesn't rage or hide.

He grieves, gives his jewels and robes to Brahmanas, sends his attendants home, and chooses the forest life of fasting and austerity. Kunti and Madri refuse to leave him. You can't call the arrow back.
You can choose the next action. Today it's the angry text you sent at midnight. Karma says it will bear fruit.

teach.h: THE NEXT ACTION IS A NEW SEED.
teach.b: It also says your next action is already a new seed.

how: Many Hindus understand both the curse and Pandu's answer through karma, action and its fruit. Ahimsa, not harming living beings, is also an important value, and stories like Kindama's are retold to show how seriously even a lawful harm can be taken.

o: a curse, like the dying sage Kindama's words
a vow to give up the throne for the forest
an arrow shot in haste while out on a hunt

p: the sage in a deer's form
the fruit of one quick arrow

s: Pandu knew the deer was a sage
the stag spoke only after the arrows struck.
karma is a god punishing you
karma means action. every action bears fruit, like a seed, and the next action is a new seed.
after the curse Pandu chose to live as an ascetic
he gave up the royal life, gave his jewels away, and sent his attendants home.

games.q: you snapped at a friend and now they've gone quiet. by Pandu's story, what does karma say?
o: it'll bear fruit, and your next action is a new seed, so act well now.
it's fate now; nothing you do changes anything.
wait for the universe to even it out.
games.why: Pandu couldn't call the arrow back, but he chose his next act: grief, gifts, the forest. karma is action, and you're still acting.

practice: Bring to mind one quick action of yours that's still bearing fruit, good or hard. Don't judge it; just see it. Then choose one next action that would plant something better.
Some Hindus offer their actions to God with a few words, like Krishnarpanam, offered to Krishna. If you pray, offer that next action. If you don't, just set it as an intention.

wordCard.voice: Shapa, a curse: the sage Kindama's dying words, the fruit of a king's quick arrow.

orig.note: Sanskrit shapa: a curse, like the one the sage Kindama speaks as he dies.

carryVoice: Your line: karma, even a quick arrow bears fruit. And the next action is a new seed. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Sambhava Parva (Kunti's self-choice; Madri; Pandu's conquests and retreat to the forest; the sage Kindama's curse; Pandu's resolve)
